children: By Fransiska Nangoy and Bernadette Christina
Extremely dry weather is disrupting coal and palm oil shipments in Indonesia's Kalimantan as water levels at key rivers receded, industry groups said on Wednesday.

Indonesia, the world's largest thermal coal and palm oil exporter, is experiencing "super-El Niño" weather conditions which have caused drought and exacerbated wildfires in Sumatra and Kalimantan, home of many of the country's coal mines and palm oil plantations.

Local media reported that the water levels of the Mahakam River in East Kalimantan, a key logistic route which stretches 980 kilometres (608.94 miles), have been receding in recent weeks. Data from Indonesia's weather agency showed that there was almost no precipitation in East Kalimantan for the whole of August.

Some members of the Indonesia Coal Miners Association in East Kalimantan on Borneo island have reported difficulties in transportation due to the river's low water levels, the group's executive director Gita Mahyarani told Reuters.
She said those members have been forced to limit the volume of coal loaded onto barges to prevent grounding.

"Consequently, the carrying capacity per trip decreases, trip frequency rises, and logistic costs increase," Gita said, adding that the extent of the impact varies by company, depending on the location of their mines and the specific sections of the waterway they need to navigate.
The group does not have an estimate of how much volume has been affected by the condition of the river.
Barges that could typically carry 7,000 metric tons were forced to lower their load to around 5,500 tons, local port authority official Mursidi told the Kompas news website on Wednesday.
He added that despite reducing their load, some barges still faced difficulties travelling upstream due to the lower water levels.
The Kapuas River in West Kalimantan also receded, affecting palm oil shipments from local planters, said Hadi Sugeng, an official with the Indonesia Palm Oil Association.
West Kalimantan contains around 10% of Indonesia's total palm oil plantation area, agriculture ministry data showed.
Around 40% of the province's output is typically shipped along the Kapuas River, Hadi said, adding that local planters are now scrambling to find alternative transportation, including trucks.
"Procuring trucking services is not an easy matter. It requires time. We are concerned that storage facilities will be full," he said, adding that transportation costs are already rising.

Currently storage tank capacity is sufficient to hold palm oil that cannot be transported, but if the disruptions last to the end of the month, it could cause issues for farmers, with mills not able to take in their palm oil fruits.
